One offer = one member-month.\n\n| Policy | Offers | Reached a churner | Wasted | Value |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| **Targeted at t\\* = 0.2143** | 242 | 62 | 180 | **+$852** |\n| — corporate | 9 | 1 | 8 | **−$78** |\n| — everyone else | 233 | 61 | 172 | **+$930** |\n| Offer to every member-month | 4,556 | 408 | 4,148 | **−$47,736** |\n| No programme | 0 | — | — | $0 |\n| *Memo: at the analyst's 0.267* | 108 | 33 | 75 | +$828 |\n\nThe quarter's total carries a standard error of **$572** — each offer returns\n+$66 or −$18, and the total is a sum of 242 such draws, so $852 sits 1.5\nstandard errors above zero.\n\n## Exhibit A3d — Where the value comes from, and where it does not\n\nSource: `analysis/outputs/a3_by_month.csv`, `a3_offer_quality.csv`.\n\n| Month | Offers | Precision | Value | Per offer |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| Oct 2025 | 114 | 21.9% | +$48 | $0.42 |\n| Nov 2025 | 81 | 33.3% | +$810 | $10.00 |\n| Dec 2025 | 47 | 21.3% | −$6 | −$0.13 |\n\n| Inside the offered set | Offers | Model says | Actually churned | Per offer |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| First contact | 195 | 28.6% | 26.2% | $3.97 |\n| Repeat contact | 47 | 28.4% | 23.4% | $1.66 |\n| Q1, just above t\\* | 61 | 22.2% | 18.0% | −$2.85 |\n| Q4, highest scores | 61 | **39.6%** | **27.9%** | $5.41 |\n\n**Figure A3** (`a3_value_curve.png`): realised value across the whole\nthreshold range, with the decision region at its own scale.\n\n---\n\n## Prose (draft, ~430 words; the recommendation above is the opening paragraph)\n\n**What the programme is worth.** Using the protocol in Exhibit A2 — admissible\ncolumns only, fitted on Jan 2024 to Jun 2025, scored once on Oct to Dec 2025 —\nthe targeting rule returns $852 on the quarter. The proposal in front of the\ncommittee says $19,774. The gap is not the threshold: applying the analyst's\nown 0.267 to honest scores returns $828, within $24 of our derived figure. The\ngap is that their number was computed on predictions that had already seen the\ncancellation, and on a random shuffle of two years rather than a fit to the\npast scored on the future.\n\n**Why the margin is thin.** An offer costs $18 and a retained churner returns\n$66, so the programme pays only while more than 21.4% of offers reach someone\nwho would have cancelled. The base rate is 9%. That requires finding members at\nroughly two and a half times the average risk, and the model manages 25.6% in\nthe top 5% of the book — profitable, but by four percentage points. Month to\nmonth that margin straddles zero: November returned $810, October $48 and\nDecember −$6. With 47 to 114 offers in a month those differences are mostly\nnoise, and that is the point — the programme sits close enough to break-even\nthat ordinary variation puts individual months on either side.\n\n**Why corporate comes out.** Corporate members were ranked below a coin flip\n(AUC 0.404 on 34 churners) and their nine offers landed on a churner once.\nThe model's single largest term is the acquisition channel itself, about four\ntimes the churn odds for any non-corporate channel, learned from 533 corporate\nrows none older than six months. It has learned that corporate members rarely\ncancel, not which of them will. Excluding them adds $78 to the quarter and\nremoves a segment forecast to triple its share of the book.\n\n**What to watch.** The threshold assumes the predicted probabilities mean what\nthey say. They roughly do — checked on the validation month, and corrected\nthere before use — but the model still overstates the risk of the members it\npicks, claiming 39.6% for its top-scoring offers and delivering 27.9%. That is\nwhat selecting the top of a noisy score does, and it is why the tripwire\nshould be a dollar figure rather than a ranking statistic: AUC can hold steady\nwhile the probabilities drift and the cut point stops meaning what it meant.\nTwo further reasons to expect less than $852 next spring: April to June ran\n5.3–7.1% churn against this quarter's 9.0%, and 1,294 members in the history\nalready received a retention contact, so part of the outcome we are fitting to\nis itself post-treatment.\n\n---\n\n## Notes to self (not memo text)\n\n### Design decisions (mine, session 4)\n\n- One offer = one member-month, matching the monthly programme and the brief's\n  per-offer economics. Per-member accounting was rejected: a churner has only\n  one flagged row, so \"which month did the single offer happen in\" has no\n  honest answer.\n- Quarter as the reporting period (the test window is exactly one quarter).\n  Monthly split added later, after it turned out to be informative rather than\n  decorative — see below.\n- Priced against offer-everyone, no programme, and the analyst's threshold.\n  Declined to score the test window with the analyst's *model*: that would be\n  a second scoring, and A2 already set the norm against it.\n- Calibration checked on the validation month and corrected there. The verdict\n  was set from validation evidence (Platt slope 0.79, under-prediction in 8 of\n  10 bins) **before** any dollar figure existed. It cost $30 — raw scores give\n  $882 — which is the point: chosen on calibration grounds, not on payout.\n- Value curve reported. It re-reads the same scores at 400 cut points; no new\n  scoring, and t* was fixed in advance. The curve peaks at $1,098 at 0.236;\n  not selecting on the test set cost $264, stated in the memo rather than hidden.\n- Recommendation shape chosen before the dollar figure was computed.\n\n### Arguing against the draft\n\n- **$852 ± $572 is 1.5 SE from zero.** A \"deploy\" that rests on it is resting\n  on a coin that landed the right way. The scoped-and-instrumented shape is\n  what the uncertainty supports; an unconditional go is not.\n- **Corporate's −$78 is nine offers and one churner.** The dollar line is\n  nearly meaningless on its own. The argument for exclusion rests on 34\n  churners at AUC 0.404, 533 training rows, and the mechanism (the model learned\n  the channel, not the members) — not on the $78.\n- **The quartile table is suggestive, not conclusive.** ~15 churners per\n  quartile; only the Q4 gap (39.6% claimed, 27.9% delivered) is about two\n  standard errors. Do not present Q1–Q3 as an established pattern.\n- **Repeat contacts are a second-order drag, not a defect.** $1.66 versus\n  $3.97 per offer, both above break-even. Worth a sentence, not a policy fight.\n  32 members were flagged more than once and never churned, costing $1,224.\n- **Seasonality cuts both ways.** Oct–Dec is a *higher*-churn quarter than\n  Apr–Jun, so the $852 is probably optimistic for deployment — but 2024 shows\n  the same summer peak, so the level is seasonal rather than a trend, and the\n  April book is not simply \"worse\".\n- **The recommendation excludes 19% of the current book and a forecast 35%.**\n  That is a large operational carve-out to justify on 34 churners. The honest\n  framing is that we cannot yet tell whether the model helps on corporate, not\n  that we know it hurts.\n\n### What changed my mind this session\n\n- I expected the monthly split to be decorative and advised skipping it (D2).\n  It turned out to carry the clearest evidence that the value is unstable, so\n  it went in. Recorded because it is exactly the kind of pre-commitment that\n  should be revisited when the data disagree.\n- I predicted that fitting the calibration on September (10.8% base rate)\n  would over-correct for a lower-rate test window. Wrong: the raw model\n  under-predicts on the test window too, because the test book is more\n  corporate and the model scores corporate low.\n\n### Trimming candidates for the two-page limit (need ~450 words out)\n\n1. A1's loss sentence — A3's break-even paragraph says it better (~40 words).\n2. A1's corporate and seasonality figures → move to exhibit footnotes (~90).\n3. A2's \"reading the rows\" row-by-row commentary → compress rows 0 and 2,\n   which moved least (~120).\n4. A2's odds-ratio prose → Exhibit A2c already carries it (~60).\n5. def load_replicates() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The controlled repeat-observation extract, and the final test set.

    Use it for two things and no others: estimating the noise floor, and
    scoring each tuned model exactly once at the end.
    """
    return pd.read_csv(DATA / "replicates.csv")


def test_extract(division: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The replicate rows for one division ('H' or 'A').  Your test set.

    Score each tuned configuration on this exactly once, at the end.
    """
    r = load_replicates()
    return r.loc[r["division"] == division].reset_index(drop=True)

Confirmed from the code: **they are the same thing.** `test_extract("H")` is a convenience wrapper that filters `replicates.csv` to division H — I checked with `.equals()` and it's byte-identical to the H slice.

```
replicates.csv        900 rows
test_extract("H")     450 rows, 45 configs × 10 replicates
test_extract("A")     450 rows, 45 configs × 10 replicates
H + A = 900           ✓
```

So there is one file doing two jobs, exactly as the brief says: "You use it for two things: estimating the noise floor, and scoring your final models once."

**And there are no hidden final models.** There are eight cells — 2 degrees × 2 treatments × 2 divisions — and every one of them gets scored on its own division's 450 replicate rows. B2 asks for "test MSE and test MSE − σ̂²" for all eight. Nothing is held back.

Strictly the replicates get used a third time, in B3: the mean of a configuration's ten replicates estimates the true mean demand at that point, which is what lets you separate bias from variance. The brief folds that into the same role — it's the ground truth, not a new test.

One structural fact worth carrying into B2, because it explains why the brief insists on "test MSE − σ̂²". Since all ten replicates of a configuration are identical on every feature, the model predicts the **same value** for all ten. So the test MSE splits exactly:

$$\text{test MSE} = \underbrace{\tfrac{405}{450}\hat\sigma^2}_{\text{noise you cannot touch}} + \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{45}\sum_g(\bar y_g - \hat y_g)^2}_{\text{how wrong the model is about the true config means}}$$

That second term is the only part a better model could remove, and it's what subtracting σ̂² is approximately recovering. Useful to be able to say out loud.

## Setting up B1

B1 is the most prescribed part of the assignment — the estimator and its standard error are both given — so there's little design freedom. Before computing, the expectations worth writing down (course doc §3):

The contractor's claim is that Apparel is *inherently* harder because its best CV MSE (414) is nearly double Hardgoods' (231). That claim is only true if Apparel's noise floor is correspondingly higher. If the two floors come out similar, then most of Apparel's 414 is **avoidable** error — a small-sample problem, not a demand problem — and the contractor has misread it. The brief's B3 note gives a hint: it says σ/√10 ≈ 4 units without distinguishing divisions, implying σ ≈ 12.6 and σ² ≈ 160 for both.

Three small calls for you:

1. **Verify the dictionary's claim that the twelve predictor fields are identical within each `config_id`?** The whole estimator rests on it — if features varied within a group, the within-group spread wouldn't be pure noise. I'd check it and assert, since it's three lines and it's the assumption doing all the work.
2. **Report σ̂ alongside σ̂²?** MSE is in units², which is hard to feel. σ̂ ≈ 12–13 units reads as "the typical week-to-week swing at an identical configuration." One extra column.
3. **Standard error only, or also a confidence interval?** The brief asks specifically for σ̂²√(2/dof). A chi-square interval would be more exact, but the brief names the approximation and comparability matters. I'd give exactly what's asked and not gold-plate it.

Confirm those three and I'll write `analysis/part2/b1_noise_floor.py`.

Your reading is right, and worth stating precisely because it's the whole argument of Part B.

Handout 1 eq. (2) splits the expected squared error at a point into a **reducible** part, (f(x) − f̂(x))², and an **irreducible** part, Var(ε | x). σ̂² estimates the second. So if both divisions have similar floors but Apparel's total error is nearly double, the excess sits entirely in the reducible term — meaning some better f̂ exists and the current one simply isn't it. One nuance to carry: "reducible" doesn't mean "easy to reduce." With 197 rows and 90 terms the reducible excess is mostly *variance*, so the lever is a better fitting **procedure** — a penalty, or fewer terms — rather than a richer model class. That's exactly what B2 measures.

**On "10 duplicates" — worth correcting, because the distinction is the assignment.** They aren't duplicates. A duplicate is identical on *every* column including `units`, which is the CO-4471 problem in `division_h.csv` that `dedup_h()` removes. A replicate is identical on the twelve recorded fields and **different on `units`**. That difference is precisely the thing we're measuring. Same file, opposite meanings: in `division_h.csv` identical rows are a pipeline fault to delete; in `replicates.csv` near-identical rows are the experiment.

**What a configuration is:** a point in twelve-dimensional feature space, not a week and not a store. The dictionary says Merchandising Analytics "identified 45 store-week configurations — distinct combinations of the twelve fields — and located ten independent weeks that matched each configuration exactly on every recorded field." So ten different store-weeks happened to land on identical recorded values. `replicates.csv` carries no `store_id` or `week_id`, so we can't tell which — and it doesn't matter, because the point is ten independent draws of `units` at the same x.

Difference (A − H) = −6.1 with a standard error of 14.4 — **0.42 standard errors**, indistinguishable from zero. Apparel's floor is if anything slightly *lower*.

**The estimator's assumption holds.** All twelve fields are constant within every one of the 90 configurations, every group has exactly ten rows, and `units` varies within every group. The script raises if any of that fails rather than computing a floor that isn't one.

**An independent check that the arithmetic is right.** The brief states, in the B3 section, that the replicate mean estimates true demand "to within about σ/√10 ≈ 4 units" — without saying which division. Ours give **3.85** and **3.77**. The brief's number was computed from data we hadn't seen and our estimate lands on it.

## What it says about the contractor

His claim was that Apparel demand is inherently harder to forecast because its best error (414) is nearly double Hardgoods' (231). The floors say the opposite: **the unpredictable part of demand is the same size in both divisions.** Both also sit at almost identical mean demand (111.9 against 111.0), so it isn't a scale effect either.

Splitting his own numbers against the floor:

| | Best CV MSE | Floor | Avoidable | Share that is floor |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Hardgoods | 231 | 148.1 | **82.9** | 64% |
| Apparel | 414 | 142.0 | **272.0** | 34% |

Hardgoods is already close to the floor — two-thirds of its error is noise nobody can remove. Apparel carries **more than three times as much avoidable error**. Same demand, same noise, different amount of error left on the table — which is a statement about the fitting procedure and 197 rows, not about Apparel's customers.

## Arguing against it

- **Homoscedasticity.** The pooled floor assumes noise doesn't grow with demand. Hardgoods shows a mild correlation between a configuration's mean and its variance (+0.24; 131 in the lowest third of means against 172 in the highest), Apparel essentially none (+0.04). So Hardgoods' floor is a slight average over a level-dependent noise. Both divisions were pooled the same way, so the comparison survives, but the single number is an average rather than a constant.
- **The 45 configurations aren't a random sample.** They're points Merchandising Analytics chose during platform validation. If they sit in an unrepresentative region of feature space, the floor there needn't be the floor everywhere. Nothing in the dictionary claims they're representative.
- **The floors could genuinely differ a little.** A 95% interval on the difference is roughly ±28 units², up to about 20% of a floor. Nowhere near enough to explain 414 against 231, but "identical" is too strong — "indistinguishable at this precision" is the defensible phrasing.

You've got it exactly right, and Handout 3 names both explicitly. §1.1, "Two levels of randomness":

> 1. the **new case** itself — specifically the noise ε₀ in Y₀ = f(x₀) + ε₀;
> 2. the **training set** 𝒟, and hence the predictor f̂ built from it.

And equation (2) keeps them in separate terms:

$$\text{Err}(x_0) = \underbrace{(f(x_0)-\bar f(x_0))^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}[(\hat f_\mathcal{D}(x_0)-\bar f(x_0))^2]}_{\textbf{Var}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}}$$

So the two variances you identified are:

| | What varies | Over what | Reducible? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Var** (the middle term) | the *prediction* f̂(x₀) | different training samples | **Yes** — more data shrinks it, ridge shrinks it |
| **σ² = Var(ε₀)** | the *outcome* Y at fixed x | repeat observations at the same x | **No** |

The dartboard in §2.3 says it in one line: Variance is "how spread out the cloud [of predictions] is"; irreducible error is "the scatter in the target itself." Same English word, different random object. **σ̂² in B1 measures the second one** — ten weeks with identical recorded features, and `units` still differs.

## Now the homoscedasticity point

Strictly, the irreducible term is Var(ε | X = x₀) — it can depend on where you are in feature space. Handout 3 §2.2 writes the population average as

$$\mathbb{E}[\text{Err}] = \overline{\text{Bias}^2} + \overline{\text{Var}} + \sigma^2$$

Notice Bias² and Var carry bars (averaged over x) and σ² doesn't. That silently assumes the floor is the same everywhere. If it isn't, that term is really σ̄² too — an *average* floor.

**Your Poisson instinct is precisely the right reference**, and Handout 1 §4.7 flags it for exactly this data type: "**Counts.** Number of claims, visits, or defects. Values are non-negative integers and the variance typically grows with the mean." `units` is a count, so variance-mean coupling is the default expectation, not an exotic worry. Let me test it properly rather than lean on the correlation, which is badly attenuated because each config's variance is estimated from only ten observations.

The test is honest and the answer is "can't tell":

| | Slope of Var on mean | Poisson (slope 1)? | Constant variance (slope 0)? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hardgoods | +0.657 ± 0.410 | consistent | also consistent |
| Apparel | +0.103 ± 0.401 | ruled out | consistent |

With 45 configurations and only ten replicates each, a single config's variance carries a standard error of about **70** on a value near 148 — nearly half. That noise swamps the relationship, which is also why the raw correlation (+0.24) understated the fitted slope (+0.66). Both divisions are mildly **overdispersed** relative to Poisson (σ̂² ≈ 1.3× the mean), so neither pure model fits.

**What this means for B1, in three lines:**

- The data are consistent with a constant floor in both divisions; Hardgoods hints at mild variance-mean coupling that the experiment can't resolve.
- It doesn't threaten the B1 comparison, because both divisions were pooled the same way over configurations spanning similar demand ranges. We're comparing two averages computed identically.
- It *would* matter if you used σ̂² to judge a single prediction at a specific store-week — the floor there could be higher or lower than 148. The memo should say "the average irreducible error," not "the irreducible error."

So your mental model is correct and complete: **σ² is nature's scatter in Y at fixed x, Var is your procedure's scatter in f̂ across samples, and only the second one responds to more data, a penalty, or a better model.** That distinction is the entire engine of Part B — B2 measures how much of each division's error sits above the floor, and B3 splits that excess into the bias and variance halves.

def oof_auc(df: pd.DataFrame, features: list[str], folds, groups=None) -> float:
    """Out-of-fold AUC with the analyst's pipeline fitted inside each fold."""
    X, y = df[features], df[TARGET].to_numpy()
    categorical, numeric = split_types(df, features)
    oof = np.zeros(len(df))
    for train_idx, test_idx in folds.split(X, y, groups):
        model = analyst_pipeline(categorical, numeric)
        model.fit(X.iloc[train_idx], y[train_idx])
        oof[test_idx] = model.predict_proba(X.iloc[test_idx])[:, 1]
    return roc_auc_score(y, oof)

Verified. Taking your questions in order.

## 1. Yes, rows 0–2 are CV on the training window — and here's the exact mechanic

[a2_evaluation.py:116-125](analysis/part1/a2_evaluation.py#L116-L125). For each of rows 0, 1, 2:

- The frame is `build` = months ≤ 2025-06, **21,031 rows** (not the validation month, not the gap months, not the test window).
- `StratifiedKFold(5)` splits it. For each fold: fit the analyst's pipeline on the other four fifths, predict the held-out fifth, store those predictions in an `oof` array.
- After five rounds every row has exactly one prediction from a model that never saw it. **One AUC is computed on the pooled 21,031 out-of-fold predictions.**

One correction to your wording: it's **AUC**, not MSE — Part A is classification. MSE is Part B. And one detail that matters for B2: we pool the out-of-fold predictions and compute a single AUC, rather than computing five fold-level scores and averaging. Both are legitimate, but only the second gives you a fold-level standard error — which is why B2 will need the other shape, since the brief asks for "CV MSE with its standard error across folds."

Row 2 differs from row 1 in exactly one thing: `StratifiedGroupKFold` with `groups=member_id`, same seed, same stratification.

## 2. The claim is accurate, with one nuance worth raising

The test I'd use: **would the choice have been different if the numbers had come out differently?**

| A2 decision | Made from | Data-driven? |
|---|---|---|
| Keep 12 columns, drop 2 | the dictionary's timing notes | No — `tenure_months` has AUC 0.50 and was kept because it's *available*; `exit_survey_started` has AUC 0.81 and was dropped because it *isn't* |
| Order 1→2→3→4 | structure (no folds exist after change 3) | No |
| `StratifiedGroupKFold(5, seed 0)` | matched the analyst's settings so the row differs by grouping alone | No |
| The model itself | `analyst_pipeline()` imported unmodified; nothing tuned | No |

So A2 chose nothing by looking at outcomes, and the validation month is genuinely untouched there — `grep` finds it mentioned only in the docstring explaining why it isn't used.

**Two precisions to carry into office hours.** First, "the validation month was never used" is true of A2 but not of Part A: **A3 used it**, to check and correct calibration, which is exactly its stated purpose. Second, the honest nuance — we *had* computed those columns' univariate AUCs in A1 before finalising A2. The decision rule was provenance, and it would have been identical without those numbers, but a strict reader could say we'd seen them.

## 3. Direct examples

**Choices made by looking at data** (these need the validation month, and make the chosen model's own score optimistic):

- Picking ridge α from `ALPHA_GRID` because it minimised CV MSE — **this is B2, and it's why Part B has a separate test extract**
- Picking polynomial degree 1 vs 2 by CV score
- Keeping the 20 features that correlate best with the outcome
- The analyst's threshold: grid-searching 400 values and taking the argmax of realised value
- Our Platt correction in A3 — fitted parameters, so it went on the validation month
- Dropping outliers because the score improved
- Trying `GroupKFold`, seeing a worse number, and going back to `StratifiedKFold`

**Choices not made by looking at data** (no validation needed):

- Dropping a column because the dictionary dates it after the scoring moment
- Grouping folds by `member_id` because a member generates many rows — a fact about the grain
- Fitting past→future because deployment predicts the future from the past
- Deriving t\* = 18/84 from the finance table
- Naming AUC as the metric before fitting anything
- Deduplicating because ticket NLF-2231 says the load was re-run
- The evaluation windows themselves — the brief fixed them

The tell in every left-column case: a number was compared, and the comparison picked the winner.

You're right that there's a pessimistic bias. There's also an optimistic one. They act on **different quantities**, which is why both can be true at once.

## Bias 1 — pessimistic, and you named it

Each CV fit sees only 4/5 of the data, while the model you deploy sees all of it. Handout 2 §3.2 says this about the single split ("Each model is fitted on only 60 weeks instead of 120... The validation estimate therefore **overstates the risk** of your final model"), and §4.3's table lists "Bias of the risk estimate: **upward**" for small K. So yes — CV is conservative about the recipe. It applies to **every candidate equally**.

## Bias 2 — optimistic, and it only exists once you select

Handout 2 §3.1, the box titled "Why the validation set cannot double as the test set":

> Once you pick the degree that minimizes validation error, the validation error **of the winner** is no longer unbiased — you selected it for being small *on that data*, which is the same selection effect that corrupts training error, **applied one level up**. The more candidates you compare, the worse it gets.

This has nothing to do with sample size or with the model seeing data during fitting. It's that the minimum of several noisy numbers is systematically below their common truth. Here it is with no model at all — 25 candidate penalties that are **genuinely identical**, true risk 400, CV noise ±30:

| Candidates compared | Reported score of "the best" | Optimistic bias |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (no selection) | 400 | 0 |
| 2 | 383 | 17 |
| 5 | 365 | 35 |
| 25 | **341** | **59** |
| 100 | 325 | 75 |

Every alpha was equally good. Reporting 341 for "the tuned model" is reporting the luckiest draw, not a better model.

## Why both hold simultaneously

They attach to different claims:

| | What it biases | Who it affects |
|---|---|---|
| **Pessimism** (sample size) | the estimate of *this recipe's* risk | every candidate equally |
| **Optimism** (selection) | the reported score *of the winner* | only the one you picked |

So for the winner: **reported score = (slightly pessimistic estimate of its recipe) − (selection optimism)**. Two errors in opposite directions, and which dominates depends on how flat the learning curve is at your *n* and on how many noisy candidates you compared.

The decisive asymmetry: **pessimism is safe, optimism is dangerous.** Being conservative about a model never causes you to deploy something bad. Being flattered does. That's the whole reason for a test set that selects nothing — and it's why, when you evaluate **one pre-specified model** on held-out data, there's no selection term at all. A2 row 3 is exactly that: one model, no candidates compared, so its 0.644 carries only the conservative bias.

## What this means for B2, concretely

Apparel makes both biases large at once: each CV fold fits on ~158 rows against 197 for the refit (steep part of the learning curve, so pessimism is real), and you compare **25 alphas × 2 degrees** on estimates that will be noisy at n=197. That's precisely why the brief pairs "CV MSE with its standard error across folds" with the one-standard-error rule — and why every cell also gets a test MSE scored once. Expect Apparel's tuned CV number to flatter itself relative to its test number, and expect the gap to be bigger in Apparel than in Hardgoods.

Now adding your two A2 caveats to the draft.

## The professor's definition

Handout 2 §4.2 defines the CV error as the **average of the K fold-level errors**, not a pooled number:

$$\text{CV}_{(K)} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\text{MSE}_k, \qquad \text{MSE}_k = \frac{1}{|F_k|}\sum_{i \in F_k} L\big(y_i, \hat f^{(-F_k)}(x_i)\big)$$

That's what you compare candidates on. And §4.5 defines the 1-SE rule on the same objects:

> Compute, along with CV_(K)(d), the standard error of the K fold-level errors, **SE(d) = sd(MSE₁,…,MSE_K)/√K**. Then select the *simplest* model whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum.

So **the 1-SE rule requires cross-validation** — the standard error comes from the spread *across folds*. A single validation set gives you one number and no spread, so there's nothing to take a standard error of.

## CV replaces the validation set; it doesn't supplement it

Handout 2 §3.2 sets up the problem with a single validation split — unstable (ten splits chose six different degrees) and biased upward (each model fitted on half the data) — and concludes: "Both problems have the same root: **we threw away half the data.** That suggests the fix." §4 is the fix. Cross-validation manufactures held-out estimates by rotating, so you no longer need to set data aside for the comparison.

The protocol in §6 does exactly this:

3. run K-fold CV **of the entire pipeline** to choose hyperparameters
4. apply the one-standard-error rule
5. refit the chosen pipeline on **all** the non-test data
6. evaluate **once** on the test set

No separate validation set. Which answers your question: you compare candidates on the CV error, not on a never-seen validation set — because under this design there isn't one.

## Why Part A has a validation month anyway

Because Part A's holdout is **temporal**, and you can't manufacture a time-ordered holdout by rotating folds. Every fold of a random CV contains future rows. So the brief gives Sep 2025 as a single time-ordered validation holdout — the temporal analogue of the validation set, used exactly once, in A3, for calibration. Part B has no such constraint (store-weeks, not a forecast origin), so it uses plain CV and the replicates are the only holdout.

## One mechanical detail that bites in B2

Pooling all out-of-fold predictions and computing one metric is **not** the same as averaging fold-level metrics — unless the folds are equal size:

| | n | Fold sizes | Pooled vs averaged |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Hardgoods | 3,000 | 600 × 5 | identical |
| Apparel | 197 | 40, 40, 39, 39, 39 | differ slightly |

A2 pooled, because AUC isn't an average of per-row losses so pooling is the natural choice there. **B2 must average**, because the brief asks for "CV MSE with its standard error across folds" and the SE only exists if you keep the five fold-level numbers. That settles the second of the four open B2 design calls — unless you'd rather do it differently.

Still open: whether the penalty is tuned to the **CV minimum** (with the 1-SE rule discussed) or tuned **by the 1-SE rule itself** — that choice also fixes what B3 freezes; whether degree 3 appears anywhere; and where Part B's figures land.

Sharp objection, and you're right that it would give you a spread. But it measures a **different quantity** — and you've independently reinvented the B3 experiment.

## The two designs measure different things

**Option A (the handout's):** model f̂⁽⁻ᵏ⁾ is scored on **its own held-out fold** F_k. Five numbers, each from a *different model* on *different data*.

**Option B (yours):** each of the five models is scored on the **same** validation set V. Five numbers, each from a *different model* on *the same data*.

The spreads answer different questions:

| | What varies | What the spread captures |
|---|---|---|
| **A** — fold errors | model *and* evaluation sample | uncertainty in the **risk estimate itself** |
| **B** — fixed V, five models | model only (V held fixed) | how much the **fitted predictor moves** with the training sample |

Option B holds the evaluation point fixed and varies the training data. That is precisely **Var** from the bias–variance decomposition — Handout 3 eq. (2), E_𝒟[(f̂_𝒟(x₀) − f̄(x₀))²]. And it is *exactly what B3 does*: `stability.py` draws 20 bootstrap resamples, refits, predicts the **same three query configurations** each time, and reports the standard deviation of the 20 predictions. Same logic, better instrumented — bootstrap resamples instead of CV folds, and a replicate-based estimate of the truth so bias comes out too.

So your instinct isn't wrong; it's the right instrument aimed at a different target. The 1-SE rule needs the uncertainty of the *estimate*, because the question it answers is "are these two CV scores far enough apart to mean anything?" Option B can't answer that — it would ignore the evaluation set's own sampling noise entirely, since every model is scored on the identical rows, so `sd(V_k)/√5` would understate the uncertainty of the mean.

## Two practical reasons it settles itself in B2

1. **Part B has no validation set.** The prescribed protocol is CV on the division's own training extract, refit, then score once on the replicates. There is no held-out V to score five models against — and borrowing the replicates for it would be selecting on the test set.
2. **Comparability.** §4.5 defines the rule as `sd(MSE₁,…,MSE_K)/√K`, so every submission computes it the same way. Using a different SE would make our 1-SE conclusions incomparable with the class's on a question the rubric grades directly.

## One honesty point worth keeping

Neither SE is exact. The five CV training sets overlap heavily — any two share three of the five folds — so the fold errors are **correlated**, and `sd/√K` is a heuristic that treats them as independent. Handout 2 §4.3 makes the same point at the other extreme for LOOCV: "the *n* models are nearly identical, so their errors are highly correlated and averaging buys little." The one-standard-error rule is explicitly "a widely used correction," justified as "models inside that band are statistically indistinguishable" — a rule of thumb for picking the simpler model among near-equals, not a hypothesis test. Worth saying in the B2 write-up when the rule does work in Apparel, since that's where several cells will land inside one band.

### Findings this session

- **The contractor's arithmetic was right; his conclusions were wrong.** All
  four of his quoted figures reproduce within half a standard error.
- **One specification serves both divisions: degree-2 ridge.** It ties the
  best hand-picked choice in Hardgoods (0.15 +/- 0.22) and beats it in Apparel
  (83.72 +/- 19.98). The 1-SE rule is what licenses the Hardgoods half.
- **Terms per row, not division size, is the quantity.** Apparel degree 1 is
  the proof: the same 197 rows, 12 terms instead of 90, penalty worth nothing
  (1.47 +/- 7.26).
- **Degree 1 -> 2 is a trade in Hardgoods and a pure loss in Apparel.**
  H: sd 1.14 -> 2.83, bias 12.65 -> 3.84. A: sd 4.33 -> 25.24, bias 16.66 ->
  18.78.
- **The penalty converts Apparel's variance problem into a bias problem.** The
  best Apparel model is 85% bias (293 against 53 units^2). So the standard
  should say "collect more Apparel history", not "use a bigger basis" or
  "penalise harder". This is the bridge into standardise-a-process.
- **CV and test diverge in opposite directions by division.** Apparel's test
  comes in below CV (158-row folds against a 197-row refit: the conservative
  CV bias); Hardgoods degree 1 goes the other way (the 45 configurations are
  not a random sample of where the training rows live).
- Two instructor-embedded checks passed: sigma/sqrt(10) ~ 4, and the tuned
  penalties coinciding at one degree and not the other.

73	
74	**Where the penalty earns its keep.** In one cell out of four, and
75	overwhelmingly: Apparel at degree 2, where the penalty takes cross-validated
76	error from 618 to 330, a drop of 288 against a standard error of 55. In the
77	other three it does nothing measurable — 0.01 in Hardgoods degree 1, 0.15 in
78	Hardgoods degree 2, 1.47 in Apparel degree 1, none of them as large as its
79	own standard error. What separates them is not the size of the division but
80	the number of terms it has to estimate per row of data: 0.46 terms per row in
81	the cell where the penalty matters, against 0.004, 0.030 and 0.061 where it
82	does not. Apparel degree 1 is the proof that "Apparel is small" is not the
83	explanation: same 197 rows, twelve terms instead of ninety, and the penalty
84	buys nothing.
85	
86	**One specification can serve both divisions.** The contractor compared
87	unpenalised fits and concluded otherwise. Allow each specification a tuned
88	penalty and degree-2 ridge is at least as good as the best hand-picked choice
89	in both: 232.98 against 233.12 in Hardgoods, a difference of 0.15 ± 0.22, and
90	329.80 against 413.53 in Apparel, better by 83.72 ± 19.98. The
91	one-standard-error rule is what licenses the Hardgoods half of that claim —
92	degree-2 ridge and the contractor's degree-2 OLS are well inside one standard
93	error of each other, so there is no evidence to prefer his, and twelve of the
94	twenty-five penalties tested sit within one standard error of the best, so
95	the exact value is not load-bearing.
96	
97	**How firm the Apparel ordering is.** Not uniformly. Apparel's standard
98	errors run 14 to 68 against Hardgoods' 4.6 to 6.4, three to ten times wider
99	on 197 rows against 3,000. Firm: degree-2 ridge beats both degree-1 cells by
100	82 to 84 with standard errors of 20 to 26, and degree-2 OLS is the worst by
101	204 ± 53. Not firm: whether to penalise at degree 1, 1.47 ± 7.26, which is no
102	evidence at all.
103	
104	**What the floor does to the reading.** Hardgoods' best leaves 99 units²
105	above its floor of 148, so roughly three-fifths of what remains is noise
106	nobody can remove. Apparel's best leaves 154 above a floor of 142: more than
107	half of its remaining error is still recoverable in principle, which is the
108	opposite of a division at its limit.

112	## Notes to self (not memo text)
113	
114	### Design decisions (mine, session 6)
115	
116	- **Tuned to the CV minimum**, not by the one-standard-error rule. The brief's
117	  question 2 asks where the rule "bears on your answer", which is a request
118	  to discuss it; one criterion across eight cells keeps them comparable; and
119	  the rule then does real work in question 2. The 1-SE α is computed and
120	  reported beside the tuned one in `b2_table.csv`.
121	  - *Correction to an earlier justification of mine.* Tuning to the CV minimum
122	    does **not** make the ridge and OLS cells comparable. It makes them less
123	    so: a ridge cell reports the minimum of 25 noisy estimates and so carries
124	    selection bias, while an OLS cell reports one estimate and carries none.
125	    Disclosed in the Exhibit B2 footnote. Evidence it is real and small: in
126	    Hardgoods degree 2, ridge wins the CV comparison by 0.15 and loses the
127	    test comparison by 1.31.
128	- **CV MSE is the average of the five fold MSEs**, not one MSE pooled over all
129	  out-of-fold predictions. The brief asks for the SE across folds, which only
130	  exists if the five are kept. Apparel's folds are 40/40/39/39/39 so the two
131	  differ slightly. (A2 pooled, correctly: it had to reproduce the analyst's
132	  protocol exactly, and AUC is a pairwise rank statistic, so the pooled
133	  version answers the deployment question of ranking one whole book.)
134	- **No degree 3.** `DEGREES` offers it and 454 terms on 197 rows would make
135	  the terms-per-row point vividly, but the brief specifies four models and
136	  says there are no marks for more. `sweep.py` shows the curve if wanted.
137	- **Figures and tables to `analysis/outputs/`**, consistent with Part A and
138	  `CLAUDE.md`, rather than the starter's script-adjacent folders.
139	- Penalties frozen to `b2_penalties.csv` for B3 to read, so B3 cannot
140	  accidentally re-tune.
141	
142	### The test MSE decomposition, and why there is nothing to footnote
143	
144	Because all ten replicates of a configuration are identical on every feature,
145	the model emits one prediction per group and the test MSE splits exactly:
146	
147	    test MSE = (405/450)·σ̂² + mean_g (ȳ_g − ŷ_g)²
148	
149	Verified to zero in all eight cells (`b2_test_decomposition.csv`). Two
150	offsetting biases, each exactly σ̂²/10:
151	
152	- The floor occupies only 405/450 of the test MSE, so subtracting a whole σ̂²
153	  removes σ̂²/10 too much.
154	- ȳ_g is itself an average of ten weeks, so it wobbles around the true mean
155	  with variance σ̂²/10, which inflates the measured gap by σ̂²/10.
156	
157	They cancel exactly, so **`test MSE − σ̂²` is the unbiased estimate of the
158	true average squared bias**. Checked: structural part − σ̂²/10 equals
159	`test MSE − σ̂²` to the cent in all eight cells. The brief's instruction is
160	exact, not approximate. Nothing to disclose; report it as asked.
161	
162	(I initially told Orcun the brief's quantity was conservative by σ̂²/10. That
163	was wrong — it ignored the noise in the replicate-mean yardstick. Recorded
164	for the process note.)
165	
166	### CV versus test diverge in opposite directions
167	
168	| Cell | CV MSE | Test MSE | Direction |
169	|---|---:|---:|---|
170	| Apparel degree 1 OLS | 413.53 | 363.58 | test **below** CV |
171	| Apparel degree 2 ridge | 329.80 | 296.19 | test below CV |
172	| Hardgoods degree 1 OLS | 336.62 | 398.55 | test **above** CV |
173	| Hardgoods degree 2 OLS | 233.12 | 246.16 | test above CV |
174	
175	Two different course ideas, one in each division:
176	
177	- **Apparel: training-set size.** Each fold fits on about 158 of the 197 rows,
178	  while the refit gets all 197, a 25% increase. CV is therefore pessimistic
179	  about the model that actually gets deployed (Handout 2 §3.2, §4.3). The
180	  effect is large here because 158 → 197 matters when there are 90 terms to
181	  estimate; in Hardgoods, 2,400 → 3,000 changes almost nothing.
182	- **Hardgoods: sample representativeness.** The gap runs the other way, so
183	  training-set size cannot explain it. The 45 replicate configurations were
184	  chosen by Merchandising Analytics during platform validation, not sampled at
185	  random from the store-week population, and degree 1 does relatively worse on
186	  them (test 398.55 vs CV 336.62) than degree 2 does (246.16 vs 233.12). The
187	  chosen points include regions a linear surface fits badly.
188	
189	Worth two sentences in §2 if the budget allows; it is not one of the brief's
190	three questions.
191	
192	### Arguing against the draft
193	
194	- **"One specification can serve both" rests on a tie, not a win.** In
195	  Hardgoods, degree-2 ridge matches degree-2 OLS in CV by 0.15 ± 0.22 and
196	  *loses* on test by 1.31. The claim is "no worse", not "better", and the
197	  memo should not overstate it. The honest framing is that standardising on
198	  degree-2 ridge costs Hardgoods nothing measurable and saves Apparel 84.
199	- **Selection bias flatters every ridge CV number.** Small where the curve is
200	  flat and the grid wide, but it is the same direction in all four ridge
201	  cells. The Apparel degree-2 gain of 288 ± 55 is far too large to be
202	  explained this way; the Hardgoods ties are exactly where it could matter,
203	  and it pushes them further towards "tie".
204	- **The contractor's arithmetic was never wrong.** All four of his figures
205	  reproduce within half a standard error. His two conclusions were wrong, not
206	  his fitting. Say so: it is a cleaner criticism and it means B1's
207	  "avoidable" column needs no restatement.
208	- **α = 10.0 is the tuned value at degree 1 in both divisions.** The curve
209	  there is nearly flat — 19 of 25 α values in Hardgoods and 16 of 25 in
210	  Apparel sit within one SE of the minimum — so the exact value is not
211	  load-bearing. But both divisions finding the *same* minimum is expected,
212	  not luck: `stability.py`'s own comment says the two divisions "land in the
213	  same place" at one degree and not the other, which ours do. (An earlier
214	  version of this note called the degree-1 argmin "close to arbitrary";
215	  too strong, corrected.) Consequence for B3, predicted before running it:
216	  degree-1 ridge and degree-1 OLS should behave almost identically. They do,
217	  to 0.01 units of sd.
218	- **Apparel's test MSE beats Hardgoods' at degree 1** (363.58 vs 398.55),
219	  which would be an odd thing to quote without the floor beside it, since the
220	  two floors are the same size. Another reason the brief insists on the
221	  subtraction.
222	- **197 rows and 5 folds means the SEs are themselves badly estimated.**
223	  sd over √5 from five correlated numbers is a heuristic (Handout 2 §4.5).
224	  "Three to ten times wider" is the right order of magnitude; do not quote
225	  Apparel's SEs to two decimals as though they were precise.

88	  instructor's, only the four models are mine.

90	  drift from B2 and cannot be re-tuned inside the resamples.

92	  the starter's `b3_outputs/` folder. This **overrides the session-1 decision**
93	  to keep the starter's folder names; one consistent output location won, and
94	  B1 and B2 already write there.
95	- **Signed mean bias added** as a column the starter does not compute. It
96	  earns its place: see the cancellation point below.
97	- **sd reported, not sd².** The brief asks for the standard deviation. Squared
98	  units appear only where proportions are being compared, and then they are
99	  computed as mean-of-squares, not square-of-mean.

104	two divisions land in the same place, and at the other they do not." Ours:

106	3.162 (A). Hint satisfied. Second embedded check Part B has passed, after
107	σ̂/√10 ≈ 4 in B1. Both are worth one line in the process note.

112	finding the same minimum is evidently expected, not luck.)
113

115	
116	Hardgoods degree-1 OLS: biases of **+21.01, −15.06, −1.89**. Mean absolute
117	12.65, signed mean **+1.35**. Reported signed alone, that model looks nearly
118	unbiased. It is not: it is a surface too rigid to bend, over-predicting low

121	Mean absolute is the right headline; signed mean is the diagnostic that
122	reveals the shape. One clause in §2 if the budget allows.

136

138	unpenalised degree-2 fit that is right — variance is the majority, 664 of
139	1,139. But **the penalty converts it into a bias problem**: Apparel's best
140	model carries 293 units² of bias² against 53 of variance. A mean absolute
141	bias of 15.05 units against a 3.77-unit yardstick is unambiguously real.
142	
143	So "Apparel is unstable, penalise it" is only half the story. The penalty has
144	already done its work; what remains is a model too rigid to follow the

150	
151	- **Twenty resamples is few.** A standard deviation from 20 draws has roughly

153	  is not a finding, and neither is 4.33 vs 4.13 in Apparel degree 1. Both are
154	  reported as "nothing", which is the honest reading, and that is also what

162	  | Same fit, the 3 query points only | 257.3 | which points |
163	  | B3: 20 bootstrap fits, same 3 points | 345.7 | which fits |
164

166	  sit at the extremes where a rigid surface fits worst. Per point, the
167	  full-data fit's reducible error is A10 = 624, A08 = −12, A07 = 159. The 45
168	  are mostly mid-range. *Which fits:* a bootstrap resample holds only about

The substance is right, but the framing would walk into the one failure the rubric names by name. From "Common ways marks are lost":

> **A "standard" that is really a model.** The VP asked for something portable to a division acquired next year. **Fixing a polynomial degree in advance has not answered her.**

So "the standard is: use degree-2 ridge" loses the point even though degree-2 ridge is the right answer *today, for these two divisions*. The repair is to separate what the standard **fixes** from what is an **output** of applying it.

## The reframing

**Degree-2 ridge is not the standard — it is what the standard produced this year.** A third division acquired next year with, say, 400 rows would run the same process and might land somewhere else, because 90 terms on 400 rows is 0.225 terms per row, between Hardgoods' 0.03 and Apparel's 0.46.

What's genuinely portable, and all of it is something we learned rather than assumed:

| The standard fixes | Because |
|---|---|
| Every error is reported against an estimated noise floor | A raw MSE has no interpretation — 414 vs 231 looked like a demand difference and wasn't |
| Each division runs a replicate exercise to get that floor | Otherwise you can't tell avoidable error from unavoidable |
| Flexibility and penalty are tuned by CV **on that division's own rows**, never hand-picked and never compared unpenalised across divisions | That is exactly the contractor's error |
| CV standard errors are reported, and the one-standard-error rule decides ties | Apparel's SEs run 14–68 against Hardgoods' 4.6–6.4; a winner declared inside that band isn't supported |
| The held-out set is scored once and selects nothing | — |
| The flexibility decision is made on **terms per row**, not on division identity or size | Apparel degree 1 proves size isn't the variable: same 197 rows, 12 terms, penalty worth nothing |

**Left to the data:** the degree, the penalty value, and therefore which of the four cells wins. Those follow from *n* and *p*, which differ by division and change every quarter.

## Your second point is supported — and I can strengthen it

You said you'd expect Apparel's bias to fall once it has enough history, because Hardgoods doesn't show it with the same model. The evidence for that is the tuned penalty itself: Hardgoods degree 2 chooses **α = 0.316**, Apparel chooses **α = 3.162** — ten times more shrinkage, same class, same twelve fields. Apparel's 293 units² of bias² is largely *shrinkage* bias that the small sample forces on it. As *n* grows, CV picks a smaller α, the shrinkage bias falls, and variance stays controlled because the sample is bigger.

Two caveats worth carrying, because the memo shouldn't overclaim:

- Handout 3 §3.2 says "more data buys variance, not bias" — true for a **fixed** class. Our argument works only because the penalty is *tuned*, so more data relaxes it. That's a two-step argument, worth stating correctly if asked.
- There's a competing explanation we can't rule out: Apparel's demand surface might simply have a different shape, in which case degree 2 is the wrong basis regardless of *n*. B1 makes the optimistic reading more plausible — same noise floor, same mean demand — but doesn't prove it. The honest version is "we expect," not "we know."

## So the §2 recommendation, for you to confirm or correct

> Standardise the **process**, not the model. Require every division to estimate its noise floor from replicates, tune degree and penalty by cross-validation on its own rows, report CV standard errors and break ties with the one-standard-error rule, and score once on held-out data. Applied today that yields degree-2 ridge in both divisions — no worse than the best hand-picked choice in Hardgoods (0.15 ± 0.22) and better by 84 ± 20 in Apparel — so one specification does currently serve both. What is not standardisable is the amount of history: Apparel's best model is 85% bias, which more flexibility and more penalty cannot fix. Its binding constraint is data volume, and the forecast is parity by late 2027.

Confirm that and I'll start drafting §1 immediately — nothing in it depends on this.

No offer is worth $0. The penalty does nothing at degree 1 in either\ndivision or at degree 2 in Hardgoods (2.83 → 2.80), and cuts Apparel's degree-2\nspread by 71%, to 7.22. Both track the same terms-to-rows ratio, 0.03 against\n0.46 — which is why the standard fixes a method rather than a specification. A\ndivision acquired next year with 400 usable rows would sit at 0.225 on the same\nninety-term basis, between these two, and the same procedure could legitimately\nselect a different degree or penalty.\n\nWhat no standard can supply is history. Apparel's best model is **85% bias** —\n293 units² against 53 of variance — while Hardgoods on the same specification\nselects a penalty ten times smaller. The shrinkage Apparel's sample forces on\nit is what creates that bias, so we expect it to fall as history accumulates\nand cross-validation relaxes the penalty. That is an expectation, not a\nmeasurement: we cannot rule out that Apparel's demand surface is simply shaped\ndifferently. Understood on the memo — I'll stop optimizing it and hand it over for you to edit. The verification script is worth finishing though, since it protects you while you edit.

**On your question: yes, with two precisions worth having.**

σ̂² estimates the irreducible error — the variation in `units` at a fixed set of recorded values that no model could predict. But:

1. **It is irreducible *given the twelve recorded fields*, not absolutely.** Handout 1 §4.3 puts the qualifier in: two cases "identical on every field the bank records" behave differently, and "no model built from **the recorded fields** can distinguish" them. If Cascade started recording a thirteenth field — local events, weather beyond mean temperature, a competitor's promotion — part of what we're calling irreducible today would become reducible tomorrow. The floor is a property of the *measurement system*, not of demand itself. That's a lever your §2 standard doesn't currently mention: more rows is one way to lower Apparel's error, more *columns* is another.

2. **It's an average over the 45 configurations that were sampled**, not over the whole store-week population. Those points were chosen during platform validation, not drawn at random, and we couldn't resolve whether the floor varies with demand level — hence "average unavoidable error" in Exhibit B1.

So the precise statement: σ̂² estimates the average, over those 45 configurations, of the conditional variance of `units` given the twelve recorded fields.

Nearly — with one word worth sharpening, because "shape of the data" could be read two ways.

σ̂² is independent of the model and of how much data you have. What it depends on is **what you measured** — which columns exist, and how `units` itself is defined and recorded. Handout 1 §4.3 puts the qualifier in the definition:

> The variability that remains **after conditioning on everything you measured** is called irreducible error, and it puts a hard floor under how well anyone can predict.

The three-way version:

| Change | Effect on σ² |
|---|---|
| Different model class, different penalty, different fitting procedure | **None** |
| More rows — 197 Apparel weeks becoming 3,000 | **None** |
| More *columns* — a thirteenth field that explains some of the within-configuration spread | **Can fall** |

So the distinction I'd be careful with: adding rows, or rows from a different part of the demand range, doesn't move the floor. Adding a *variable* can. That's why the replicate design works at all — ten weeks identical on all twelve fields still differ in `units`, and the only way to explain that difference is to record something you aren't currently recording.

**This matters for §2's standard.** The two levers are genuinely different interventions:

- *More Apparel weeks* lowers the **reducible** error — it lets cross-validation relax the penalty, which is what shrinks that 293 units² of bias.
- *More fields* lowers the **floor itself** — and Hardgoods sits only 99 units² above a floor of 148, so the remaining headroom there is small. If Cascade wants materially better Hardgoods forecasts, the lever is measurement, not modelling.

That second point is arguably the strongest thing your §2 could add, and it's the sort of claim that survives being applied to a third division: a standard that requires every division to report its distance from its own floor automatically tells you which lever that division needs.
